analysis.one_liner: Allows high interest rates on bank loans to survive even after the loan is sold to non-bank lenders.
analysis.headline: The bill never received a hearing, vote, or cosponsor and died in the House Financial Services Committee when the 114th Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: Federal law lets national banks charge the highest interest rate allowed in their home state, even if that rate exceeds the cap in the borrower's state. This bill would extend that privilege to whoever buys the loan later — so a bank could make a loan at, say, 200% interest and sell it to a non-bank lender, which could keep charging that rate no matter what the borrower's state law says. In practice, this is the legal foundation of 'rent-a-bank' arrangements, where high-cost lenders rent a bank's charter to dodge state rate caps. The bill was referred to committee and went no further.
analysis.who_benefits: Non-bank consumer lenders and fintech companies that partner with banks to make loans, because they could buy or service loans carrying a bank's home-state interest rate and keep charging it anywhere, overriding state usury caps. Banks gain a new revenue stream selling loan origination to these partners.

how_it_helps.text: Amends two federal banking laws to say that once a bank loan is valid as to its interest rate when made, that rate remains valid even if the loan is sold, assigned, or transferred to a third party.
This would let bank-originated loans escape state interest-rate limits in the borrower's state after transfer, because the federal 'valid when made' rule would follow the loan rather than state law.

The sponsor described this as protecting consumers' access to credit — the argument being that guaranteed enforceability of bank rates keeps credit flowing to borrowers whom state caps would price out of the market.

analysis.who_pays: Borrowers in states with low interest-rate caps, especially small-dollar and subprime borrowers, who could face rates set by a bank's home state rather than their own — often far higher than their state allows. State governments lose their ability to enforce local rate caps on these loans.
analysis.who_pays_short: Borrowers in states with rate caps

drawbacks.text: The bill would override state interest-rate caps for a large class of consumer loans, since a bank could originate a loan at any rate lawful in its own state and sell it onward; borrowers in capped states would lose that protection.
It provides the legal underpinning for 'rent-a-bank' lending, in which non-bank high-cost lenders use a bank partner's federal rate authority to charge rates the borrower's own state forbids.

Defenders of state caps argue this shift removes the main tool states have to police predatory lending, and that the bill had no Democratic cosponsors and received no committee action — signs of how contested the approach was.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit is smoother, more predictable credit markets for bank lending partners and, arguably, continued credit availability for some risky borrowers. The cost falls on borrowers in states with low rate caps, who could be charged far higher rates than their own laws allow. Because the bill's main mechanism is removing state-level consumer protection, the tradeoff is heavily tilted toward lenders.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the House Financial Services Committee and sat there with no hearing, no markup, and no floor vote until the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Representative Patrick McHenry introduced the bill on July 11, 2016, with no cosponsors.
The same day, it was referred to the House Committee on Financial Services.
No further action was ever taken on it, and the 114th Congress ended on January 3, 2017, killing the bill.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Because the bill died, state interest-rate caps remained enforceable against transferred loans and high-cost lenders did not gain a federal route around them. Borrowers in capped states are better off than they would have been under the law the bill proposed.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Borrowers protected by state rate caps

for.name: Patrick McHenry
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and referred it to committee; it was his sole sponsorship, with no cosponsors.

against.name: House Committee on Financial Services
against.what_they_did: Received the referral on the day of introduction and took no further action — no hearing, no markup, no report — before the Congress ended.

sides.party_line_note: No votes were ever taken and the bill attracted no cosponsors of either party, so the record shows only a single Republican sponsor and no demonstrated support or opposition.

industries.note: The bill would let these lenders buy bank-originated loans and keep charging the bank's home-state rate, bypassing state caps in the borrower's state. This is the core of rent-a-bank small-dollar lending.
Banks gain a saleable loan product with guaranteed rate enforceability, creating fee income from origination-for-sale arrangements. Borrowers using the loans directly from the bank see no change.

industries.industry: State usury-cap enforcement (state regulators and capped-state borrowers)
industries.note: The bill removes the practical effect of state rate caps for any loan touched by a bank sale or assignment, weakening states' main anti-predatory-lending tool.
